extracted.intended_audience: the people of the State of New York; citizens and ratifiers debating the proposed U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and evaluative principles for structuring the Executive and Judiciary in the proposed U.S. Constitution, focusing on appointment mechanisms, tenure, independence, safeguards, and the proper scope of federal judicial power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment: Presidential nomination with Senate concurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Power of nomination is vested in the Executive and subject to the judgment/consent of the Senate (nomination by President; appointment with Senate's concurrence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This separation produces transparency and clear responsibility: nominations are public and submitted to an entire legislative branch, so the blame for a bad nomination falls on the President, while the censure for rejecting a good one lies with the Senate. The right of nomination yields many of the benefits of appointment while avoiding many of its evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid small private councils for making appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Councils of appointment composed of a few persons, meeting privately, are improper for distributing offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such small closed bodies are vulnerable to cabal and intrigue, lack public inspection, facilitate bargaining and vote‑trading, enable manipulation (e.g., regulating meeting times to avoid opposition), encourage monopolies of office among families, and undermine responsibility and public confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not vest appointment power in the House of Representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: A fluctuating and numerous body like the House is unfit to exercise the appointment power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the House may grow very large and is mutable, giving it appointment power would defeat advantages of stability in the Executive and Senate and create infinite delays and embarrassments; historical state practice supports rejecting this idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated executive functions (limited and specific authorities)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Executive's remaining powers include informing Congress of the state of the Union; recommending measures; convening one or both houses on extraordinary occasions; adjourning them when they cannot agree on adjournment; receiving ambassadors and public ministers; faithfully executing the laws; and commissioning officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the ordinary and proper functions of the Chief Magistrate; objections to these specific authorities (except a few cavils about convening and reception of ambassadors) are insubstantial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks on the Executive: election, impeachment, prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Executive is checked by election (President elected once in four years by persons chosen by the people for that purpose), by impeachment and trial, and by subsequent prosecution in the ordinary course of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These precautions (regular election, liability to impeachment and removal, disqualification from other offices, and exposure to later prosecution) together secure due dependence on the people and due responsibility of the Executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial tenure during good behavior (life tenure barring misconduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: All judges appointed by the United States shall hold their offices during good behavior (i.e., effectively for life unless removed for misconduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life tenure under 'good behavior' is endorsed as one of the most valuable modern improvements: it secures a steady, upright, and impartial administration of the laws and is a primary means to keep the judiciary independent from executive and legislative encroachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanency in office is indispensable to judicial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanency (continuance in office) is essential because the judiciary is naturally the weakest department and must be enabled to defend itself against the other branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the judiciary has 'neither force nor will' and depends on the executive to enforce its judgments, permanency is the citadel of public justice and security; without it courts are in jeopardy of being overpowered, awed, or influenced by co‑ordinate branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts must be able to declare legislative acts void when contrary to the Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Every act of a delegated authority that is contrary to its commission (the Constitution) is void; courts must disregard statutes that contravene the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine does not make the judiciary superior to the legislature; it affirms the superiority of the people's will (the Constitution) to that of their agents. Courts enforcing this are bulwarks of a limited Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts as interpreters of the Constitution (fundamental law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution is a fundamental law and it belongs to the judges to ascertain its meaning as well as that of ordinary statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts act as an intermediate body between the people and the legislature to keep the latter within assigned limits; the interpretation of laws is the proper and peculiar province of the judiciary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for resolving conflicting laws: time and hierarchy distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: When two statutes conflict, courts ordinarily prefer the later in time; but where a statute conflicts with the Constitution (a superior authority), the Constitution prevails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'last in time' rule is a construction rule among equals, not derived from positive law. Between superior and subordinate authority, the prior superior act governs, so courts must adhere to the Constitution over contradictory statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence protects against transient popular passions and unjust laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence of the courts is required to guard the Constitution and individuals' rights from the ill humors and passing passions of society or designs of interested men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent judges temper and confine the operation of unjust or partial laws, serve as a check that discourages legislators from pursuing iniquitous intentions, and preserve public and private confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial compensation must not be diminished during continuance in office
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges shall at stated times receive compensation which shall not be diminished during their continuance in office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents the legislature from using salary diminishment to influence judges; compensation may be varied to accommodate changes in value of money, but a judge's pay may not be reduced relative to what it was at appointment. (Distinction noted: President's compensation cannot be increased or diminished; judges' can be increased but not diminished.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment is the appropriate mechanism for judicial responsibility; avoid removal for inability or rigid age limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges are accountable by impeachment (House impeaches, Senate tries) for malconduct; removal on grounds of inability or fixed age limits is neither practical nor desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisions to remove judges for 'inability' invite abuse because mental faculties are hard to measure; arbitrary or partisan removals would undermine independence. Age limits (e.g., New York's limit of 60) are criticized as improper because deliberative faculties often persist beyond such ages and dismissal on that basis is inhumane and unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanency attracts experienced, learned judges and preserves legal continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Because extensive precedents and complex law require long and laborious study, permanency in office is necessary to attract and retain men of sufficient learning and integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary duration would discourage competent practitioners from accepting the bench, worsening the quality of justice; hence permanence encourages the development and preservation of a robust body of precedents and legal skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper extent of the federal judicature (jurisdiction categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal judiciary ought to extend to: (1) cases arising under laws of the United States passed pursuant to constitutional powers; (2) cases concerning execution of the articles of Union; (3) cases in which the United States is a party; (4) cases involving the peace of the Confederacy, including intercourse with foreign nations and between the States; (5) causes originating on the high seas and of admiralty or maritime jurisdiction; (6) cases in which State tribunals cannot be supposed to be impartial and unbiased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories ensure a constitutional method of enforcing national prohibitions on states, preserve uniformity in interpreting national laws (avoiding thirteen independent final courts), provide proper fora for controversies involving the nation or foreign parties, secure the public faith in international intercourse, and supply a remedy where state courts are partial.
